summary: Specifies a simple method for IMAP and POP servers to serve internationalized messages to conventional clients. It is easy to implement but gives only rudimentary results.

eli5.summary: A quick, simple way to translate fancy-letter emails so old mail programs can still show them, though the result is a bit rough.

questions: how do servers send utf-8 mail to old mail clients
what is the imap downgraded response code
how do imap servers show utf-8 email to old clients
what is a surrogate message in email
subtitle: A deliberately simple way for IMAP and POP servers to show internationalized mail to old clients, with some information lost.

tldr.problem: Conventional IMAP and POP clients cannot handle internationalized messages, yet hiding the whole message is unhelpful when the subject, text and attachments could be shown.
tldr.mechanism: The server synthesizes a surrogate message: internationalized addresses are replaced with invalid ones, unpresentable MIME parameters and header fields are dropped, and the subject is encoded as RFC 2047 if needed.
tldr.outcome: It is easy to implement but gives only rudimentary results, and signatures, message references and the original addresses may be lost. It updates RFC 3501 on message sizes and adds a DOWNGRADED IMAP response code.

today: RFC 6858 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2013 that updates RFC 3501. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, and the text encourages clients to implement UTF-8 support instead.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
A conventional IMAP or POP client may open a mailbox with internationalized messages, for example when a user has both internationalized and conventional mail clients. Address-based operations are rarely possible, including displaying addresses, replying, and most address-based signatures. The sender's name, subject, body and attachments can still be displayed.

The server is assumed to store internationalized messages natively. For a conventional client it synthesizes a surrogate message. The RFC values simplicity over fidelity, because a high-fidelity algorithm such as the one in RFC 6857 is likely more work than proper UTF-8 support for POP (RFC 6856) and IMAP (RFC 6855).
sections.eli5: An old mail program cannot read some new emails. The server makes a simpler copy that shows the main parts, even if some bits are missing.

sections.title: What Is Preserved and What Is Lost
sections.content: The surrogate message conveys the most important information. Where information is lost, the user should consider the message incomplete rather than modified. It is not meant to give client software any signal that would require or enable special handling. Client authors who want to handle internationalized messages are encouraged to implement UTF-8 support for POP and IMAP.
sections.eli5: If something is missing, you should think of the letter as torn, not rewritten. Better readers can ask for the full version.

sections.title: Replacing Internationalized Addresses
sections.content:
Each internationalized address in the listed header fields is replaced with an invalid email address whose display name tells the user what happened. The display-name format is explicitly unspecified: anything that tells the user what happened is good, and anything that produces an address that might belong to someone else is bad.

For Fred Foo <fred@EXAMPLE.com> the RFC offers examples such as Fred Foo <invalid@internationalized.invalid> or the group form fred:;. The .invalid top-level domain is reserved, so such addresses never belong to anyone. The affected fields are Bcc:, Cc:, From:, Reply-To:, Resent-Bcc:, Resent-Cc:, Resent-From:, Resent-Sender:, Resent-To:, Return-Path:, Sender: and To:. Addresses in other fields, such as Received:, are not treated as addresses.
sections.eli5: A name tag with fancy letters is swapped for a note saying that an address was here, using a made-up address that nobody owns.

sections.title: MIME Parameters, Subject and Other Fields
sections.content:
Any MIME parameter, in the message header or a body part header, that cannot be presented exactly as it arrived is silently excised. For example, Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=FOO is presented as Content-Disposition: attachment.

If the Subject field cannot be presented exactly, the server presents a representation encoded as specified in RFC 2047. Any other header field that still cannot be presented is silently excised.
sections.eli5: Labels that cannot be copied properly are left off. The subject is wrapped in a code so it survives the trip.

sections.title: IMAP and POP Specifics
sections.content:
RFC 3501 requires the size returned for a message to be exact. This RFC relaxes that: when a conventional client asks for size information, an IMAP server may return the size of the internationalized message even though the surrogate differs. When the server downgrades while generating FETCH responses, it reports which messages were synthesized with a DOWNGRADED response code carrying a set of UIDs. This can help humans debugging the server or client.

DOWNGRADED does not necessarily list every internationalized message in the mailbox, only those downgraded for that request. In POP, the line count in the TOP command refers to the surrogate message, while sizes reported by commands such as LIST may refer to either version.
sections.eli5: The server may tell you the size of the original letter, not the copy, and it can say which letters it rewrote.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an internationalized message has a signature covering header fields, the surrogate's signature almost certainly is invalid and may be invalid in other cases. It should still not be removed, to preserve as much information as possible. Excised information does not reach the recipient; notably Message-Id: and References: may be excised, which can remove context.

Clients such as Fetchmail download messages and delete the server copies, so the surrogate may become the only remaining version and information is permanently lost. Clients that cache messages for a very long time, such as the stock Android client, must take care not to use an old surrogate from the cache instead of retrieving the real message after being internationalized.
sections.eli5: If a copy replaces the original and the original is thrown away, the missing bits are gone for good. Old copies should not be kept once a better reader arrives.

data.code:
C: a UID FETCH 1:* BODY.PEEK[HEADER.FIELDS(To From Cc)]
S: 1 FETCH (UID 65 [...]
S: 2 FETCH (UID 70 [...]
S: a OK [DOWNGRADED 70,105,108,109] Done
